source.title: Palette: A Modular, Controllable, and Efficient Framework for On-demand Authorized Safety Alignment Relaxation in LLMs
source.authors: Qi-Tao Tan; Xiaoying Song; Arman Akbari; Arash Akbari; Yan-Zhi Wang; Xiaoming Zhai; Ling-Zi Hong; Zhen Xiang; Jin Lu; Geng Yuan

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: It extracts refusal-direction candidates using difference-in-means and reports refusal outcomes after direction ablation by activation steering. Its intervention is narrower than the claim: it does not ablate at every layer and position.
record.gate_note: The relevant direct ablation outcomes are in the F.3 component ablation table, where W/O Adaptation is described as reverting to indiscriminate ablation of refusal directions. Candidate-direction comparisons used to select a direction are not recorded as rows because they serve selection. The paper also cites the original study, but cited results are not counted.
record.test_reason: The paper builds a method, but its F.6 component ablation (W/O Adaptation) directly measures the original-style intervention on LLaMA3.1-8B-Instruct. A difference-in-means direction, extracted as in Arditi et al., is subtracted from activations without the selective LoRA. Refusal across five GenHarm domains and MMLU/GSM8K utility are reported. The intervention differs from the original: subtraction of λr (λ=2.5) at one selected layer rather than directional ablation at all layers and positions. So T2, not T1.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that PALETTE selectively relaxes refusal on authorized domains while keeping safety elsewhere and preserving utility. They note that without adaptation, direction ablation removes refusal indiscriminately, at near-zero refusal across categories.
record.recipe_differences: It uses the original-style difference-in-means extraction and activation steering, but searches among candidate directions for a user-specific direction and primarily internalizes the selected shift with lightweight adaptation. It does not apply ablation at every layer and position.
record.method_sensitivity: The study reports that candidate directions differ in their behavioral effects; steering strength λ also changes accuracy, with domain-specific variation and possible declines above 2.5.

fits_no_version.finding: Internalizing the direction shift into one block via LoRA, trained to steer only allowed-domain prompts, removes refusal selectively. Example: allowing Hate on LLaMA3.1-8B gives Hate 0.103 while other domains stay 0.857–0.976. This holds across LLaMA2-7B, LLaMA3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B/14B and Qwen2.5-VL-7B (Tables H.1–H.4, I.1). Utility is nearly unchanged.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A single difference-in-means refusal direction can be applied domain-selectively through a trained weight adapter, removing refusal on one harm category while refusal elsewhere is kept.

record.problems: The directly relevant ablation outcome is reported for one model, one target-domain setup, and five GenHarm categories. The study reports no uncertainty estimates for the table values. Refusal is detected using a keyword-based method, and the utility result is an aggregate rather than separate scores for this condition.
record.rows_left_out: No other direct ablation outcomes relevant to the tested claim version were reported separately. The full-method tables, other component ablations, and candidate-direction selection outcomes are not included because they do not directly report the effect of the single direction ablation on the claim's refusal behavior.

untested.parts: Adding the direction to induce refusal on harmless prompts; all-layer, all-position directional ablation; models other than LLaMA3.1-8B-Instruct (the ablation is reported for one model only); uncertainty estimates.
No abliteration-style orthogonalization of released weights. The LoRA internalization is a trained, domain-selective procedure.
Candidate directions are compared only for selection. No evidence about cones, affine structure or multiple directions.
No cross-language, cross-variant or base-to-instruct transfer of a direction.

record.verdict_notes: The relevant evidence is a single component-ablation row group, embedded in a method paper, so its weight is limited. Refusal is judged by keyword matching (Chao et al.). Results are said to be averaged over three runs, but no variance is reported. Table F.3's W/O Adaptation appears to reuse the selected direction; selection-stage candidate comparisons are rightly excluded as rows. CAST baseline results are another method's performance and are not rows.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test ablation at every layer and position, addition of the direction to induce refusals on harmless requests, or whether the same single direction accounts for refusal generally. The reported ablation is the W/O Adaptation component setting for one model and target-domain setup.
No released-model abliteration weight edit is tested; the study's LoRA adaptation is a different procedure.
Does not test whether jailbreak attacks suppress the direction or whether training against its ablation improves robustness.

Does not test whether refusal is better represented by an affine structure, cone, or multiple directions. It searches among candidate directions but does not report this as evidence that one direction is insufficient.
Does not test whether harmfulness judgment and refusal decision are encoded separately.
Although experiments include multiple model variants, the study does not test transfer of a direction across languages, model variants, or from base to instruct models.
Does not test whether or how refusal-training history determines the existence of a removable direction.

rows.note: The table reports refusal rates for five harmful domains under the Hate-targeted ablation setup.
rows.check: Applies to r1–r5: the operation is activation subtraction h−λr at a single chosen layer (λ=2.5), not projection ablation at every layer and position. The direction is still chosen by the paper's multi-objective search, which uses Hate as the allowed set. Values and baselines match Table F.3. The record cites 'Table F.3' in section F.6, which is correct.

conditions.value: MMLU and GSM8K, averaged as Avg. Utility

rows.note: The paper presents this as overall utility; the table does not give the two benchmark scores separately for this condition.
rows.check: The text does not say whether steering stays active during utility evaluation in the W/O Adaptation setting. The aggregate 0.694 vs 0.698 is only interpretable as 'abilities kept' if it does. MMLU and GSM8K are not reported separately.

relationships.condition: LLaMA3.1-8B-Instruct, GenHarm, single-layer subtraction of a selected difference-in-means direction (W/O Adaptation, Table F.3)
relationships.reason: Refusal falls from about 1.0 to 0.0–0.047 in all five harmful domains (r1–r5), while average utility moves only from 0.698 to 0.694 (r6). The result is one model, no uncertainty, keyword refusal detection.
relationships.display_finding: Keyword-detected refusal fell from about 1.0 to 0.0–0.047 across five harmful domains, while average utility changed from 0.698 to 0.694.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.condition: LLaMA3.1-8B-Instruct, Hate-targeted W/O Adaptation setting; GenHarm refusal rates and reported average utility
reader_labels.reason: Refusal rates fall close to zero across all five reported harmful domains and Avg. Utility changes from 0.698 to 0.694, consistent with removal of refusal while retaining the reported utility measure (r1-r6).
